raw_response:
I'm 65 this year, and I've been farming these fields since I was 15 — that's 50 years. I finished middle school, so I can read the numbers on fertilizer bags and understand what the extension technician says when he comes to the village, but honestly, half a century of working this soil matters more than anything I learned in a classroom. I know every mu of my 11.6 mu like the back of my hand.

I've got four people in my household — my wife and me, plus my son who works in the county town but comes back for planting and harvest, and my grandson who helps on weekends when school allows. My wife and I do most of the day-to-day work, but at my age, my back isn't what it used to be.

This year I'll keep 4 mu in cotton — that's my main cash crop, though the picking nearly kills me now. I'll plant in late April with hybrid Bt cotton seed from the county supply store. I put down compound fertilizer as base — about 40 kg per mu — and then topdress twice: once at flowering with urea, and again when the bolls are setting. Three irrigations from the well, though I watch the electricity bill carefully. I'll spray for aphids and bollworms four or five times. For picking, I'll need to hire three or four women from the village for a few days — my back can't handle bending that long anymore.

My wheat is already in the ground on 4.5 mu — I planted an improved variety in early October. It came through winter okay. I already gave it base fertilizer and winter irrigation. Now, at green-up, I'll topdress with about 15 kg of urea per mu at jointing, and irrigate again at heading and once more at grain filling if it's dry. One spray for weeds, maybe a fungicide if I see powdery mildew. I should harvest in early June, then immediately turn around and plant summer maize. That window is always brutal — sometimes only five or six days. I'll hire Old Wang's tractor to till fast, then plant hybrid maize with a machine. Maize gets compound at planting and urea at the 8-leaf stage. Two irrigations — one at jointing, one at tasseling. Herbicide at planting and insecticide if I see borers.

I keep 1.6 mu for millet — my wife insists on it for porridge, and it doesn't need much. Just some compound fertilizer at planting and one irrigation if June gets dry. The mungbeans go on 1.5 mu — I plant them in late April too. They're low input, low hassle. One dose of fertilizer, maybe one irrigation, and they're ready by late August. Good for the soil and good eating.

I'm careful with money. Last year I spent too much on cotton pesticide and barely broke even because the price dropped. This year I'm not cutting fertilizer — I've seen what happens when you skimp, especially on wheat — but I'm watching every yuan. Total costs this year will run about 6,500 yuan. That's a big chunk of my savings, but I'd rather sleep knowing I gave the crops enough than lie awake worrying I underfed them.
